title: Quantum Secure Time Transfer for Satellites
authors: Ravi Singh Adhikari, Anju Rani, Aman Gupta, Xiaoyu Ai, Robert Malaney
abstract: We experimentally demonstrate an entanglement-based Quantum-Secure Time Transfer (QSTT) system in an emulated low Earth orbit satellite-to-ground channel using a type-0 Sagnac-based entangled-photon source. Our new QSTT system delivers a finite Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) key rate of approximately $3~$bits$~\text{s}^{-1}$ with a $10^{-10}$ security parameter, providing a $30$-fold increase in the QKD key rate compared to the state-of-the-art entanglement-based QKD system delivered by the Micius satellite. Beyond this high key rate outcome, novel to our QSTT system is a GPS-free clock synchronization, optimized use of QKD, embedded post-quantum security, and obfuscation of the system configuration via use of a pre-shared key. Collectively, these enhancements deliver the most efficient and secure deployment of QSTT to date, and point the way forward to high-accuracy ultra-secure time transfer in space.
summary: This paper presents an experimental Quantum-Secure Time Transfer (QSTT) system designed for satellite communication. By leveraging entanglement-based photon sources and integrating Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), the system achieves unprecedented key rates and high clock synchronization precision. This advancement establishes a new benchmark for ultra-secure, space-based timing services.
main_problem: The primary goal is to establish a highly secure and precise time synchronization method over satellite-to-ground channels, overcoming vulnerabilities and precision limits of classical timing protocols.
main_result: The developed Quantum-Secure Time Transfer (QSTT) system achieved a QKD key rate of approximately 3 bits s-1, representing a 30-fold increase over state-of-the-art Micius satellite demonstrations.
method: The system combines entanglement-based quantum signaling for time transfer with Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) to encrypt time-tag data, incorporating post-quantum security and obfuscation techniques.
model_or_system: The experiment uses an entanglement-based QSTT system emulated in a low Earth orbit channel, utilizing a type-0 Sagnac-based entangled-photon source (EPS) built with a PPKTP crystal.
key_observables: QKD Key Rate (3 bits s-1), Clock Offset (sub-nanosecond precision), and Timing Jitter ($\sigma_{ex} = 473$ ps).
important_parameters: 30-fold increase in QKD key rate vs. Micius; $10^{-10}$ security parameter; $\sim 2$ orders of magnitude increase in EPS rate using type-0 crystal.
main_assumptions: The protocol assumes the use of QKD keys to seed symmetric encryption (like AES) rather than encrypting all data with a One-Time Pad (OTP) due to rate mismatch.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the overall QSTT system schematic, while Figure 2 details the experimental setups for both the EPS and the full QSTT system.
paper_structure: The paper details the physical setup (EPS using type-0 PPKTP), the QSTT protocol which involves data alignment and fine synchronization, and the security enhancements using QKD and post-quantum cryptography.
why_interesting: The work demonstrates advanced quantum networking protocols applied to time synchronization, which is a critical application area for quantum information science, particularly concerning secure communication over long-haul links.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: The QSTT system. A satellite with an onboard entangled photon source distributes entangled photons to Alice and Bob’s ground stations. Timing data is generated locally by both parties from the photon’s detection. Alice encrypts the timing data using the method described in Section II-B and transmits it to Bob via a classical communication channel. Upon receiving Alice’s encrypted timing data, Bob decrypts it, performs clock synchronization using his and Alice’s timing information, and corrects his time tag using the estimated clock offset. The pump and the generated entangled photons are represented by blue and red rays, respectively.
